trace.final_message:
The timestamps in `events.csv` use mixed time zone conventions. That's the likely cause of the hours-long jumps.

| id | ts | offset |
|----|----|--------|
| 1 | `2026-03-01T10:00:00Z` | UTC |
| 2 | `2026-03-01T10:05:00` | **none** |
| 3 | `2026-03-01T04:10:00-06:00` | -06:00 (equals 10:10Z) |

**Rows with no offset:** id 2 is the only one.

Rows 1 and 3 are consistent with each other. In UTC they are 10:00 and 10:10, so they sit about 10 minutes apart. Row 2 has no offset, so a parser has to guess. Depending on the tool, it will read the row as UTC, as local time, or as a naive timestamp that can't be compared with the zoned ones. If the data was meant to be UTC, that row lands in the right place. If it's really local time from a source in a different zone, it shifts by that zone's offset. Mixed naive and aware values can also make some libraries (pandas, for example) coerce them to strings or fail. Any of these can move events by several hours on a chart.

Row 3 is also a risk. Anything that drops the offset and keeps `04:10` will put that event 6 hours early.

**Suggested fixes:**
1. Find which system writes the offset-less rows and what zone it uses. I can't tell that from the file.
2. Make that writer emit an explicit offset, or `Z`.
3. In the chart code, parse with `utc=True` (or the equivalent) after assigning the right zone to the naive rows. Don't let the parser guess.

The file has only 3 rows, so it may be a sample. I can scan the full dataset if you point me to it. I can also look at the chart code to see how it parses `ts`.
